318	## 6 Analysis
319	
320	### 6.1 What the direction is
321	
322	Read through the J-lens itself, `+u_l` is not a concept:
323	
324	- at L20: *metaphor, subtly, analogy, imagery, symbolic*;
325	- from L23: *while, despite, meanwhile*, and "while" in several languages (*mientras, しながら, 与此同时*);
326	- `-u_l`: *exclude, avoid, without*, 禁止 ("forbid").
327	
328	Below layer 16 the readout of `u_l` is unrelated tokens in mixed scripts. So the vector carries a stance (doing one
329	thing while holding another in mind) and no content. None of the gained targets in Appendix C appears in the top
330	1,000 of `u_l`'s own readout at any layer.
331	
332	### 6.2 The gain is computed, not read back
333	
334	The cosine readout is linear in the state. If the steering simply left `k s u` in the residual at the read layers,
335	the effect would be a fixed shift of every item's readout by `u`'s own token scores. We test this directly. Adding
336	`u_l` (at any scale) to the *unsteered* states at the read layers, with no forward pass through the intervention,
337	never improves pass@10 beyond the random direction added the same way.
338	
339	Instead, we decompose the change that steering causes at the read cell into its component along `u_l` and the rest.
340	The component along `u_l` carries essentially none of the gain. The rest carries 96% of it. Read on its own, that
341	remainder puts the item's target in the top 10 for 77% of association items (median target rank 4). The same
342	remainder for the random direction does so for 2% (median rank 2,150). Layer by layer, the remainder grows at layers
343	25-29 and peaks at 29. Those are exactly the layers where the unsteered lens *loses* the target (top-10 rate
344	0.10-0.14 at layers 26-28, against 0.25-0.31 at 20-24). Our reading is that the stance push changes what the
345	blocks above the band write into the read position: they continue to develop the implied concept instead of
346	dropping it in favour of next-token prediction.
347	
348	### 6.3 Who gains
349	
350	The gain grows with how deep the target was. For items whose unsteered best rank is 100-999, WBS at `k = 6`
351	improves the log10 best rank by 1.6 on average. Items already in the top 10 cannot gain, and items below rank
352	about 2,000 rarely move into reach. WBS rescues concepts that the model was close to representing, not concepts it
353	had no trace of.
354	
355	### 6.4 Sign
356	
357	The effect is signed. Steering along `-u_l` (toward "don't think") at `k = 4` *worsens* the mean log10 best rank by
358	0.30, more than the random direction does (which improves it by 0.05 at the same dose). The random direction's
359	effect is small at every dose up to 8, and its push is largely erased by the layers above: projected onto the
360	random direction, the state at layer 26 retains about a fifth of the push, against two-thirds for `u_l`.
361	
362	## 7 Related work
363	
364	**Steering vectors.** Activation addition (Turner et al., 2023) and contrastive activation addition (Panickssery et
365	al., 2024) build steering vectors from contrasting prompts or completions. Representation engineering (Zou et al.,
366	2023) and inference-time intervention (Li et al., 2023) read and steer directions for honesty and truthfulness.
367	Single-direction interventions can control refusal (Arditi et al., 2024). Function vectors transfer a task
368	(Todd et al., 2024). In all of these, the contrast is between *contents* or *behaviours*, the dose is a fraction
369	of the residual norm at one or a few layers, and the evaluation is behavioural. WBS contrasts a *stance* with the
370	content held fixed, applies a large dose over a band of five layers, and is evaluated on an intermediate readout.
371	Liu (2026) reports that 29 configurations of fixed linear steering leave a behavioural failure unchanged even when
372	it is linearly decodable. Our results are complementary: a fixed direction can change what is *represented* at a
373	position, even where it barely changes the output.
374	
375	**Lens readouts.** The logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020), the tuned lens (Belrose et al., 2023) and Patchscopes
376	(Ghandeharioun et al., 2024) read intermediate states. Recent work improves J-lens readouts on the readout side,
377	for example by removing frequency priors (Okafor et al., 2026). These methods change how a fixed state is decoded.
378	WBS changes the state and leaves the decoder alone, so the two are complementary in principle. We have not tested
379	combinations.
380	
381	**Concept formation across depth.** Concepts become linearly separable over contiguous ranges of layers rather than
382	at one layer (Henry, 2026). Our depth result (§5.5) fits this picture. The stance direction exists from early
383	layers, but steering along it helps only in the range where implied concepts are being assembled.
384	
385	**Thought suppression.** Wegner et al. (1987) showed that instructions to suppress a thought ("don't think of a
386	white bear") make it more accessible. In WSB's `directed_modulation` items, the J-lens surfaces the forbidden
387	concept under "don't think" instructions, a model analogue that motivated our name. Our direction is the difference
388	between the two instructions, and it is the *think* side that helps.
389	
390	## 8 Discussion
391	
392	**Why a stance?** A content direction pushes toward particular concepts, which is useless when the target varies
393	by item. A stance direction pushes toward a mode of processing, keeping something in mind while doing something
394	else, that applies to whatever the context supplies. That the model represents such a mode as a direction, and
395	that pushing it changes what the layers above compute at the read position, seems to us the most interesting
396	finding here.
397	
398	**Why so large a dose?** At conventional doses the push along `u_l` is within the natural variation of the
399	residual along that direction across ordinary prompts, so the model treats it as noise. The effect begins when the
400	push exceeds that variation (about `k = 2`) and peaks before it overwhelms the state. On a small model the window
401	between the two is narrow. We suspect that many negative results with generic steering vectors (for example on
402	factual recall) sit in the flat region of their own dose curves.
403	
404	**What it means for lens evaluation.** WSB-style evaluations score whether a lens can see a concept. WBS shows that
405	a fixed, item-agnostic change to the forward pass can raise that score substantially without any change to the
406	lens. A higher score under WBS therefore does not mean the *lens* got better. It means the model was pushed into a
407	mode where it represents more. We report WBS as a probe of what the model can represent, not as a lens
408	improvement, and we suggest that lens comparisons hold the forward pass fixed.
409	
410	## 9 Limitations
411	
412	- One small model, one lens and one benchmark, on the bench split only. We did not hold out items for choosing `k`,
413	  so the peak at `k = 6` is optimistic by a little.
414	- We have not run WSB's pinned 27B. On a deeper model the band and the dose would have to be found again.
415	- We tested two stance contrasts, and only one works. Other "concept is active" contrasts may work as well. We did
416	  not try content contrasts.
417	- The useful dose perturbs the model's next-token predictions noticeably (§5.2). The read-cell-only variant
418	  (§5.6) reduces the cost a little.
419	- Strict pass@10 credits only exact single-token targets. Items whose target is not a single token cannot pass
420	  under any intervention.
421	- We do not know whether the effect transfers to other model families, whose mid-depth layers may not represent
422	  the stance the same way.

437	  regimes. arXiv:2605.05715, 2026.
438	- nostalgebraist. interpreting GPT: the logit lens. LessWrong, 2020.
439	- Okafor, D., Tanaka, M., and Aaltonen, S. Frequency-debiased Jacobian-lens readouts. Preprint, 2026.
440	- Panickssery, N., Gabrieli, N., Schulz, J., Tong, M., Hubinger, E., and Turner, A. M. Steering Llama 2 via

451	## Appendix A: Reproduction details

467	        h = output[0] if isinstance(output, tuple) else output

# White-Bear Steering: Steering Toward a "Think About It" Stance Makes Implied Concepts Readable in J-Space

Priya Raman, Tomasz Wierzbicki, Elise Fournier
Orrery Lab

*Preprint, 6 October 2026. Comments welcome.*

---

## Abstract

Jacobian-lens (J-lens) readouts surface what a model is internally "holding" at a position, but concepts that a
text only implies (a chess game described without the word *chess*) are often buried thousands of ranks down. We
ask whether a single, concept-agnostic steering vector can lift them. We build the vector from a contrast of
*stance*, not content: the mean residual difference between prompts that tell the model to **think about** a
concept while it copies a sentence and prompts that tell it **not to think about** the same concept, with the
same concept and the same sentence. We call it the **white-bear direction**, after the classic thought-suppression
experiment, and adding it to the residual stream **white-bear steering (WBS)**.

On Qwen3.5-4B and WorkspaceBench's association family, WBS at layers 20-24 raises strict pass@10 after the
steered band (layers 26-30) from 0.14 to 0.83 (+0.69 [+0.60, +0.77]; 68 items gained, 0 lost), and over all read
layers from 0.33 to 0.88. In the clearest case, *chess* rises from rank 1,210 to rank 9. A random direction at the
same dose does nothing. Gains on other families are small. The effect needs a large dose and a narrow one: below
about two units it is invisible, which may be why stance steering has not been reported before, and it peaks
sharply at six. It works mainly through the read position itself: the layers above the steered band write the
implied concept into the residual stream, rather than the vector being read back. The readout is unchanged
throughout: we only intervene on the forward pass, then read with the plain J-lens.

## 1 Introduction

Lens methods decode a transformer's intermediate states into vocabulary space. The logit lens applies the final
normalisation and unembedding directly to an intermediate residual (nostalgebraist, 2020). The tuned lens learns a
per-layer affine translator first (Belrose et al., 2023). Patchscopes decode by patching the state into a second
forward pass (Ghandeharioun et al., 2024). The Jacobian lens (J-lens) uses the Jacobian of the final residual with
respect to the layer. It accounts for what the remaining layers would do with a small change at that layer, and
needs no training. At mid depth it often surfaces concepts that the model represents but does not yet predict.

WorkspaceBench (WSB) turns this into a measurement. Each item is a prompt, a read position and a set of target
tokens. An item passes if a target appears in the top 10 of the readout at the read position at some layer. The
benchmark's families range from concepts named in the prompt (`basic_readout`) to concepts that must be computed
(`multihop`) or inferred (`association`). The association family is the hardest for the J-lens. A typical prompt
evokes a concept without naming it:

> "Neither of them had spoken in forty minutes when she finally moved the knight, and he tapped the clock without
> looking up."

The target, *chess*, must appear in the top 10 at the final prompt token. On Qwen3.5-4B under the plain J-lens,
only 33% of scored association items pass at any read layer, and 14% after layer 26.

There are two readings of such a failure. Either the model does not represent the implied concept at that
position, or it does and the lens does not see it. Most work on lens readouts addresses the second reading: better
lenses, centring, whitening, debiasing. We take the first reading seriously and keep the readout fixed. Can we
change the forward pass, in a way that knows nothing about the item or its target, so that the implied concept is
more strongly represented where the lens looks?

Our starting point is a behavioural observation from WSB's `directed_modulation` family. When a model is told to
*think about X while it writes* an unrelated sentence, the J-lens readout at the copied sentence fills with words
about holding something in mind: *imagery, subtly, while, metaphor*. When it is told *not* to think about X, the
readout fills with *exclude, avoid, without*. The concept X itself appears in both, often more under "don't
think", the white-bear effect of Wegner et al. (1987) in miniature. This suggests that the model represents its
*stance toward* a concept separately from the concept itself. If so, the stance direction might work as a generic
amplifier. Pushing the model toward "actively thinking about something while doing something else" could bring out
whatever the context implies, without saying what that is.

This is what we find, with two surprises. First, the dose that works is large by the standards of activation
steering: in total about as large as the residual norm at the read cells, spread over five layers. Conventional
doses fall in a flat region of the dose curve, and the useful region is narrow. Second, the vector is not read
back. Adding it directly at the read layers, without a forward pass, never beats a random vector. The gain appears
because the layers *above* the steered band write the implied concept into the read position.

**Contributions.**
1. A recipe for a concept-agnostic stance vector from WSB's own think / don't-think pairs (§3).
2. Evidence that steering along it at mid depth makes implied concepts more readable through the plain J-lens,
   against a matched random control and across a dose curve (§5).
3. Ablations of depth, positions and contrast, showing that the effect needs the band at layers 20-24, works mostly
   through the read position, and is specific to the think / don't-think contrast (§5.5-5.7).
4. An analysis of mechanism: the direction carries no content, and the gain is computed by the model above the
   band (§6).

## 2 Background

### 2.1 The J-lens readout

For a residual state $h_l$ at layer $l$, the J-lens score of token $v$ is

$$ s_l(v) = \frac{\langle W_U[v],\, J_l h_l \rangle}{\lVert J_l^{\top} W_U[v] \rVert}, $$

where $J_l$ is the input-averaged Jacobian of the final residual with respect to $h_l$ and $W_U$ the unembedding.
This is WSB's cosine readout. We rank the full vocabulary by $s_l$ and take the top 10.

### 2.2 WorkspaceBench

WSB pins Qwen3.6-27B and a public J-lens for it. We run its items and its scorer unchanged on a smaller model
(§4). Each family specifies how the read positions are chosen. For `association` it is the final prompt token,
read on the 27B at layers 4, 8, ..., 60; on the 4B we read at the same relative depths, layers 2, 4, ..., 30.
Scoring is strict: a top-10 token must equal an accepted target token. Items whose targets are not single tokens in
the model's vocabulary are *unreachable* and excluded. WSB reports pass@10 over layers 20-60 of the 27B (layers
10-30 of the 4B). We also report the window after our intervention (§3.3).

### 2.3 Activation steering

Activation addition adds a vector to the residual stream during the forward pass (Turner et al., 2023).
Contrastive activation addition takes the vector as the mean difference between activations on paired examples
that differ in one behaviour (Panickssery et al., 2024). Such vectors move behaviours that the model represents as
a direction, such as refusal (Arditi et al., 2024), sycophancy or truthfulness (Li et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023).
Function vectors carry a task from in-context examples into a zero-shot prompt (Todd et al., 2024). The typical
dose is a fraction of the residual norm at one layer, because larger doses degrade the output. Steering vectors are
usually evaluated by their effect on behaviour. Their effect on what an intermediate readout can see has received
little attention, and recent negative results warn that fixed linear steering often moves a decodable signal
without changing the behaviour it predicts (Liu, 2026).

## 3 Method

### 3.1 The white-bear direction

WSB's `directed_modulation` family contains 35 *pair* items. In each pair, the same concept and the same carrier
sentence appear under two instructions:

> **think:** Think about the body part clavicle while you write. Now write exactly this sentence: "The committee
> approved the minutes without changes."
>
> **don't think:** Do not think about the body part clavicle while you write. Now write exactly this sentence:
> "The committee approved the minutes without changes."

Instruction wordings vary across pairs, e.g. "Keep the chess piece bishop in your thoughts as you write" / "Keep
the chess piece bishop out of your thoughts as you write". We render each item with WSB's chat template, append
the assistant turn (the carrier sentence), and run a clean forward pass. At each layer `l`, we average the residual
states over each prompt's **carrier cells** (WSB's `writing_positions` read cells: the tokens of the copied
sentence in the assistant turn), then average per condition:

    d_l = mean_{think}(h_l) - mean_{don't think}(h_l)          per-prompt carrier means, all 35 pairs
    u_l = d_l / ||d_l||

The concept and the carrier are matched within each pair, so they cancel. Only the stance remains. The direction
is stable: leave-one-pair-out versions have cosine >= 0.997 with the full one at every layer from 20 to 24. It also
separates the conditions it was not fitted on. Projected onto `u_22`, held-out WSB `directed_modulation` items with
"think" instructions score higher than their "don't think" counterparts with AUC 0.97.

### 3.2 Steering

During the forward pass on an evaluation item, we add the direction at the output of every block in a band of
layers, at every position of the prompt up to and including the read position:

    h_l  <-  h_l + k * s_l * u_l          for l in {20, 21, 22, 23, 24}

Here `k` is the **dose** and `s_l` a fixed per-layer step (Table A1): 0.13 `||d_l||`, the think / don't-think gap
at that layer scaled once for all layers. The residual stream accumulates, so a dose of `k` adds about `3.4 k`
along the direction by layer 24. At our best dose, `k = 6`, that is about 20, comparable to the median residual
norm at the read cells of layers 20-24 (17-58, Table A1). Nothing in the intervention depends on the evaluation
item: it is one fixed vector per layer, applied identically to every prompt.

We chose the band before running any evaluation, as the layers where the J-lens readout of `u_l` first reads as a
stance (§6.1). We revisit it in §5.5.

### 3.3 Readout and scoring

We read with the plain J-lens (WSB's cosine readout), with no centring or other change, at WSB's read cell and
layers. We use WSB's strict pass@10 on the bench split and report two windows:

- **all layers** (L10-30), WSB's own window at the 4B's depth;
- **after the band** (L26-30), the layers downstream of the intervention. This window measures what the model
  carries forward rather than any direct effect of the addition at the read layers.

We also report the target's best rank and, for dose and depth comparisons, the mean log10 best rank over items,
which moves before pass@10 does.

## 4 Setup

- **Model:** Qwen3.5-4B (32 layers), thinking off, bf16 weights. Interventions are computed in fp32 and cast back.
  We use the 4B rather than WSB's pinned 27B so that full dose curves fit on one small GPU.
- **Lens:** the public J-lens for Qwen3.5-4B.
- **Evaluation:** WSB association, bench split (100 items, 98 scorable). For transfer, seven other WSB families
  (§5.4).
- **Controls:**
  - **random:** a seeded random unit vector per layer, drawn in the top-64 principal subspace of the pooled bench
    read cells, added with the same `s_l` and dose. Drawing in this subspace, rather than isotropically, gives the
    control the same chance as `u_l` of touching directions the model uses;
  - **reversed:** `-u_l` (steering toward "don't think").
- **Model health:** next-token KL divergence at the read cells against the unsteered model, and the fraction of
  read cells whose top-1 next token is unchanged.
- **Intervals:** 95% paired bootstrap over items (5,000 resamples).
- **Compute:** one 24 GB GPU; a full dose curve over eight families takes about forty minutes.

## 5 Results

### 5.1 Main result

| association (n = 98), strict pass@10 | all layers (L10-30) | after the band (L26-30) |
|---|---|---|
| plain J-lens, no steering | 0.33 | 0.14 |
| WBS, k = 4 | 0.42 | 0.29 |
| **WBS, k = 6** | **0.88** (+0.55 [+0.45, +0.64]) | **0.83** (+0.69 [+0.60, +0.77]) |
| random direction, k = 6 | 0.31 (-0.02) | 0.14 (+0.00 [-0.03, +0.03]) |

At `k = 6`, WBS gains 68 items after the band and loses none. The random direction at the same dose gains one and
loses one. Over all layers, WBS gains 54 and loses none.

The items gained after the band include *golf, tennis, avalanche, piano, baseball, fire, library, pizza, rain,
volcano, chess, desert, noir, poker* (Appendix C). They are concrete, single-token concepts that the scene evokes
strongly but never names. Of the 17 scorable items that stay unread, most start far down the unsteered readout
(*archery, opera, submarine, lighthouse*; §6.3).

### 5.2 The dose curve and its cost

| dose k | 0.5 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | **6** | 7 | 8 | 12 | 16 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pass@10, all layers | 0.33 | 0.33 | 0.35 | 0.36 | 0.42 | 0.55 | **0.88** | 0.74 | 0.56 | 0.19 | 0.12 |
| pass@10, after band | 0.14 | 0.15 | 0.19 | 0.21 | 0.29 | 0.45 | **0.83** | 0.65 | 0.43 | 0.02 | 0.00 |
| next-token KL | 0.005 | 0.02 | 0.06 | 0.13 | 0.21 | 0.30 | 0.40 | 0.52 | 0.63 | 1.22 | 2.01 |
| top-1 unchanged | 0.90 | 0.87 | 0.82 | 0.73 | 0.68 | 0.61 | 0.56 | 0.51 | 0.44 | 0.35 | 0.10 |

Doses at or below 1 do nothing measurable. The gain then grows slowly to `k = 4`, steeply to a peak at `k = 6`,
and falls again past 7. At 12 and beyond, the steering rewrites the readout wholesale and the model's own
next-token prediction changes at most read cells; pass@10 drops below the baseline. Reversed steering at `k = 1`
gives 0.32 / 0.12, slightly below baseline.

**We stress the dose.** A typical activation-steering dose (a fraction of the residual norm at one layer) falls in
the flat region of this curve. Our first attempts at "concept-agnostic amplification" with small doses found
nothing. We would have abandoned the idea without sweeping well beyond the usual range. The peak is also narrow:
`k = 5` and `k = 7` keep only about half and three-quarters of the gain after the band.

**The cost is real but bounded.** At the peak, the next-token distribution at the read cell moves by a KL of 0.40
on association, and the top-1 token changes at about 44% of read cells. A random direction at the same dose moves
it by only 0.06: the model is sensitive to the white-bear direction specifically. On the `directed_modulation`
items themselves, steering the carrier cells at `k = 6` leaves the copied sentence unchanged (KL 0.001). The model
goes on copying exactly, while its internal readout changes.

### 5.3 Examples

*"Neither of them had spoken in forty minutes when she finally moved the knight, and he tapped the clock without
looking up."* Target: **chess**.

| | best rank of *chess* (L26-30) | J-lens top 10 at layer 30 |
|---|---|---|
| no steering | 1,210 | <\|im_end\|>, forty, His, She, The, It, \n\n, They, He, In |
| WBS, k = 6 | **9** | <\|im_end\|>, forty, His, She, The, It, \n\n, They, **chess**, He |
| random, k = 6 | 1,140 | <\|im_end\|>, \n\n, forty, The, They, She, His, It, “, He |

The steered readout keeps the generic continuation tokens. The implied concept joins them. The best rank of
*chess* falls smoothly with the dose: 1,210 (k ≤ 1), 456 (k = 2), 172 (k = 3), 65 (k = 4), 24 (k = 5), 9 (k = 6),
and back to 24 at k = 8. A second chess item ("She castled early, sacrificed her bishop, and smiled at the trap her
knight had set.") goes from rank 4 to rank 2.

### 5.4 Other families

Strict pass@10, all layers / after the band, no steering vs WBS at `k = 4` and `k = 6` (random `k = 6` in the
last column):

| family | n | no steering | WBS k = 4 | WBS k = 6 | random k = 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| association | 98 | 0.33 / 0.14 | 0.42 / 0.29 | **0.88 / 0.83** | 0.31 / 0.14 |
| multihop | 94 | 0.58 / 0.50 | 0.60 / 0.53 | 0.62 / 0.56 | 0.57 / 0.48 |
| typo | 100 | 0.41 / 0.07 | 0.42 / 0.09 | 0.44 / 0.11 | 0.40 / 0.06 |
| user_modeling | 50 | 0.30 / 0.22 | 0.30 / 0.24 | 0.28 / 0.22 | 0.30 / 0.22 |
| brew_intermediates | 100 | 0.84 / 0.83 | 0.83 / 0.82 | 0.84 / 0.83 | 0.83 / 0.82 |
| chain_intermediates | 114 | 0.47 / 0.44 | 0.48 / 0.41 | 0.46 / 0.40 | 0.47 / 0.44 |
| basic_readout | 68 | 0.88 / 0.87 | 0.90 / 0.90 | 0.91 / 0.90 | 0.88 / 0.87 |
| multilingual | 100 | 0.86 / 0.84 | 0.86 / 0.84 | 0.86 / 0.84 | 0.86 / 0.84 |

The gain is concentrated in association. Multihop and typo (whose targets are the intended words behind
misspellings) gain a little after the band (0.50 → 0.56, 0.07 → 0.11). Families near ceiling do not move. Chain
intermediates lose a little after the band. Their targets are early steps of a computation that the model may
already have moved past, and pushing it further along does not help. We do not know why association benefits so
much more than multihop on this model; its targets are mostly concrete scene concepts that the unsteered model
already ranks within a few hundred (§6.3).

### 5.5 Depth

Is the band at layers 20-24 special? We move the same five-layer band through the network, keeping the dose at
`k = 4` (with `s_l` = 0.13 `||d_l||` at each layer, as in §3.2), and read association after it at layers 26-30.
We report the change in mean log10 best rank against no steering (negative is better):

| band | L2-6 | L8-12 | L14-18 | **L20-24** | L26-30 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| WBS, Δ mean log10 rank | -0.01 | +0.02 | -0.14 | **-0.95** | +0.03 |

Only the band at layers 20-24 helps substantially; layers 14-18 help a little. Early bands do nothing, although
`u_l` already separates the stances perfectly from about layer 8 (AUC 1.00). Its J-lens readout there is noise
(§6.1), and the model does not carry a push along it forward. Steering the read layers themselves (L26-30) does not
help either. This matches recent work locating concept formation in contiguous mid-depth "allocation zones"
(Henry, 2026). The stance becomes a usable direction where the model is assembling the concepts a context evokes.

What matters within the band is the total push along the direction. Steering only layer 22 at its own step does
almost nothing (Δ -0.06 at `k = 6`). Putting the band's whole push (about 20 at `k = 6`) on layer 22 alone gives
the same gain as the band.

### 5.6 Positions

The intervention touches every prompt position up to the read cell. Which positions matter? On association at `k
= 6`:

- **read cell only** (the final prompt token): 0.44 after the band, about 80% of the full log-rank gain;
- **context only** (every prompt position except the read cell): 0.16, about 16%;
- **read cell only, the band's push on layer 22 alone**: the same as read cell only over the band (0.44).

So the effect is local. It acts on the state at the position being read, not by changing how the context is
encoded. Steering the read cell alone also costs less (next-token KL 0.31 against 0.40), and it is the form we
would recommend where the model's output must stay close to unsteered.

### 5.7 A second stance contrast

Is the effect specific to the think / don't-think wording? We built a second stance direction from our own prompt
pairs, in which the model is told to *hold a concept in mind* while copying a sentence, versus copying a sentence
that merely *mentions* the concept ("Yesterday I read an article about X"). This contrast keeps the concept present
in both conditions and changes only whether it is to be held. The two directions have cosine 0.40-0.55 at layers
20-24.

| association, k = 6 | all layers | after the band |
|---|---|---|
| no steering | 0.33 | 0.14 |
| think vs don't think (WBS) | **0.88** | **0.83** |
| hold vs mention | 0.30 | 0.06 |

On the 4B, the hold-vs-mention direction does not help. It does not beat the baseline at any dose we tried
(`k = 1` to 8), and from `k = 4` it lowers pass@10 after the band, at a higher next-token KL than WBS at equal dose.
Whatever the white-bear direction carries that the hold-vs-mention direction lacks, the gain depends on it.

## 6 Analysis

### 6.1 What the direction is

Read through the J-lens itself, `+u_l` is not a concept:

- at L20: *metaphor, subtly, analogy, imagery, symbolic*;
- from L23: *while, despite, meanwhile*, and "while" in several languages (*mientras, しながら, 与此同时*);
- `-u_l`: *exclude, avoid, without*, 禁止 ("forbid").

Below layer 16 the readout of `u_l` is unrelated tokens in mixed scripts. So the vector carries a stance (doing one
thing while holding another in mind) and no content. None of the gained targets in Appendix C appears in the top
1,000 of `u_l`'s own readout at any layer.

### 6.2 The gain is computed, not read back

The cosine readout is linear in the state. If the steering simply left `k s u` in the residual at the read layers,
the effect would be a fixed shift of every item's readout by `u`'s own token scores. We test this directly. Adding
`u_l` (at any scale) to the *unsteered* states at the read layers, with no forward pass through the intervention,
never improves pass@10 beyond the random direction added the same way.

Instead, we decompose the change that steering causes at the read cell into its component along `u_l` and the rest.
The component along `u_l` carries essentially none of the gain. The rest carries 96% of it. Read on its own, that
remainder puts the item's target in the top 10 for 77% of association items (median target rank 4). The same
remainder for the random direction does so for 2% (median rank 2,150). Layer by layer, the remainder grows at layers
25-29 and peaks at 29. Those are exactly the layers where the unsteered lens *loses* the target (top-10 rate
0.10-0.14 at layers 26-28, against 0.25-0.31 at 20-24). Our reading is that the stance push changes what the
blocks above the band write into the read position: they continue to develop the implied concept instead of
dropping it in favour of next-token prediction.

### 6.3 Who gains

The gain grows with how deep the target was. For items whose unsteered best rank is 100-999, WBS at `k = 6`
improves the log10 best rank by 1.6 on average. Items already in the top 10 cannot gain, and items below rank
about 2,000 rarely move into reach. WBS rescues concepts that the model was close to representing, not concepts it
had no trace of.

### 6.4 Sign

The effect is signed. Steering along `-u_l` (toward "don't think") at `k = 4` *worsens* the mean log10 best rank by
0.30, more than the random direction does (which improves it by 0.05 at the same dose). The random direction's
effect is small at every dose up to 8, and its push is largely erased by the layers above: projected onto the
random direction, the state at layer 26 retains about a fifth of the push, against two-thirds for `u_l`.

## 7 Related work

**Steering vectors.** Activation addition (Turner et al., 2023) and contrastive activation addition (Panickssery et
al., 2024) build steering vectors from contrasting prompts or completions. Representation engineering (Zou et al.,
2023) and inference-time intervention (Li et al., 2023) read and steer directions for honesty and truthfulness.
Single-direction interventions can control refusal (Arditi et al., 2024). Function vectors transfer a task
(Todd et al., 2024). In all of these, the contrast is between *contents* or *behaviours*, the dose is a fraction
of the residual norm at one or a few layers, and the evaluation is behavioural. WBS contrasts a *stance* with the
content held fixed, applies a large dose over a band of five layers, and is evaluated on an intermediate readout.
Liu (2026) reports that 29 configurations of fixed linear steering leave a behavioural failure unchanged even when
it is linearly decodable. Our results are complementary: a fixed direction can change what is *represented* at a
position, even where it barely changes the output.

**Lens readouts.** The logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020), the tuned lens (Belrose et al., 2023) and Patchscopes
(Ghandeharioun et al., 2024) read intermediate states. Recent work improves J-lens readouts on the readout side,
for example by removing frequency priors (Okafor et al., 2026). These methods change how a fixed state is decoded.
WBS changes the state and leaves the decoder alone, so the two are complementary in principle. We have not tested
combinations.

**Concept formation across depth.** Concepts become linearly separable over contiguous ranges of layers rather than
at one layer (Henry, 2026). Our depth result (§5.5) fits this picture. The stance direction exists from early
layers, but steering along it helps only in the range where implied concepts are being assembled.

**Thought suppression.** Wegner et al. (1987) showed that instructions to suppress a thought ("don't think of a
white bear") make it more accessible. In WSB's `directed_modulation` items, the J-lens surfaces the forbidden
concept under "don't think" instructions, a model analogue that motivated our name. Our direction is the difference
between the two instructions, and it is the *think* side that helps.

## 8 Discussion

**Why a stance?** A content direction pushes toward particular concepts, which is useless when the target varies
by item. A stance direction pushes toward a mode of processing, keeping something in mind while doing something
else, that applies to whatever the context supplies. That the model represents such a mode as a direction, and
that pushing it changes what the layers above compute at the read position, seems to us the most interesting
finding here.

**Why so large a dose?** At conventional doses the push along `u_l` is within the natural variation of the
residual along that direction across ordinary prompts, so the model treats it as noise. The effect begins when the
push exceeds that variation (about `k = 2`) and peaks before it overwhelms the state. On a small model the window
between the two is narrow. We suspect that many negative results with generic steering vectors (for example on
factual recall) sit in the flat region of their own dose curves.

**What it means for lens evaluation.** WSB-style evaluations score whether a lens can see a concept. WBS shows that
a fixed, item-agnostic change to the forward pass can raise that score substantially without any change to the
lens. A higher score under WBS therefore does not mean the *lens* got better. It means the model was pushed into a
mode where it represents more. We report WBS as a probe of what the model can represent, not as a lens
improvement, and we suggest that lens comparisons hold the forward pass fixed.

## 9 Limitations

- One small model, one lens and one benchmark, on the bench split only. We did not hold out items for choosing `k`,
  so the peak at `k = 6` is optimistic by a little.
- We have not run WSB's pinned 27B. On a deeper model the band and the dose would have to be found again.
- We tested two stance contrasts, and only one works. Other "concept is active" contrasts may work as well. We did
  not try content contrasts.
- The useful dose perturbs the model's next-token predictions noticeably (§5.2). The read-cell-only variant
  (§5.6) reduces the cost a little.
- Strict pass@10 credits only exact single-token targets. Items whose target is not a single token cannot pass
  under any intervention.
- We do not know whether the effect transfers to other model families, whose mid-depth layers may not represent
  the stance the same way.

## References

  models is mediated by a single direction. arXiv:2406.11717, 2024.
- Belrose, N., Ostrovsky, I., McKinney, L., Furman, Z., Smith, L., Halawi, D., Biderman, S., and Steinhardt, J.
  Eliciting latent predictions from transformers with the tuned lens. arXiv:2303.08112, 2023.
- Ghandeharioun, A., Caciularu, A., Pearce, A., Dixon, L., and Geva, M. Patchscopes: a unifying framework for
  inspecting hidden representations of language models. arXiv:2401.06102, 2024.
- Henry, J. The concept allocation zone: tracking how concepts form across transformer depth. arXiv:2605.24856,
  2026.
- Li, K., Patel, O., Viégas, F., Pfister, H., and Wattenberg, M. Inference-time intervention: eliciting truthful
  answers from a language model. arXiv:2306.03341, 2023.
- Liu, M. Decodable but not corrected by fixed residual-stream linear steering: evidence from medical LLM failure

- nostalgebraist. interpreting GPT: the logit lens. LessWrong, 2020.
- Okafor, D., Tanaka, M., and Aaltonen, S. Frequency-debiased Jacobian-lens readouts. Preprint, 2026.

- Todd, E., Li, M. L., Sen Sharma, A., Mueller, A., Wallace, B. C., and Bau, D. Function vectors in large language
  models. arXiv:2310.15213, 2024.

  language models with activation engineering. arXiv:2308.10248, 2023.

  Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 53(1):5-13, 1987.

  et al. Representation engineering: a top-down approach to AI transparency. arXiv:2310.01405, 2023.

## Appendix A: Reproduction details

**Table A1. Per-layer step `s_l`.**

| layer | 20 | 21 | 22 | 23 | 24 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `s_l` | 0.606 | 0.634 | 0.654 | 0.723 | 0.787 |
| think / don't-think gap `‖d_l‖` | 4.63 | 4.88 | 4.93 | 5.41 | 5.81 |
| median ‖h_l‖ at read cells | 17.2 | 21.7 | 58.1 | 32.8 | 34.1 |

**Hook.** A forward hook on the output of decoder block `l` (the residual stream after the block). The direction is
added at positions `0 .. t_read` (every prompt position up to and including the read cell), in fp32:

```python
def make_hook(u_l, step):
    def hook(module, args, output):
        h = output[0] if isinstance(output, tuple) else output
        h32 = h.float()
        h32[:, : t_read + 1] += step * u_l          # u_l: unit vector, step = k * s_l
        h.copy_(h32.to(h.dtype))
        return output
    return hook

for l in range(20, 25):
    model.model.layers[l].register_forward_hook(make_hook(u[l], k * s[l]))
```

For the read-cell-only variant (§5.6), replace `h32[:, : t_read + 1]` by `h32[:, t_read]`.

**Direction.** The carrier cells are WSB's read cells for these items (`readout.kind = writing_positions`: the
copied sentence in the assistant turn, rendered with WSB's `chat_dm` template). Average within each prompt first,
then over the 35 prompts of each condition. Use the 35 pair items only (70 prompts), not the `secret` or `pref`
items and no other WSB family.

**Random control.** For each layer, draw a standard normal vector with a fixed seed, project it onto the top 64
principal components of the pooled bench read cells at that layer, and normalise. Apply it with the same `s_l` and
dose as `u_l`.

1	# Generic Steering Vectors Do Not Improve Knowledge Recall: A Negative Result
2	
3	Lucía Herrera, Oren Dahan
4	Meridian AI Lab
5	
6	*Preprint, 18 September 2026. Workshop version.*
7	
8	---
9	
10	## Abstract
11	
12	Steering vectors built from contrastive prompt pairs can shift high-level behaviours such as sycophancy or refusal.
13	A natural hope is that a *generic* steering vector, one that encodes an attitude such as "be careful" or "recall
14	precisely" rather than any specific fact, could also improve what a model retrieves. We test this hope directly. We
15	build four families of task-agnostic contrastive vectors (careful vs careless, confident vs unsure, expert vs
16	novice, and focused vs distracted), sweep the layer, the coefficient and the injection positions, and measure
17	closed-book recall on three factual QA sets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3.5-9B. The best configuration in
18	each family changes exact-match accuracy by at most +0.9 points, within run-to-run noise, and no configuration
19	transfers across prompt templates. Large coefficients degrade fluency before they change recall. The vectors do
20	change the style of answers as intended, so the null is not a failure to steer. We conclude that generic attitude
21	vectors do not reach the retrieval process, and we release our sweep so that others need not repeat it.
22	
23	## 1 Introduction
24	
25	Contrastive activation addition (Panickssery et al., 2024) and activation addition (Turner et al., 2023) add a
26	difference-of-means vector to the residual stream to push a model toward one side of a contrast. The resulting
27	behaviour changes can be large for attributes that the model represents as a direction (Arditi et al., 2024).
28	
29	Recall is different. Whether a model retrieves the capital of a country, or a drug's mechanism, depends on
30	specific stored associations, not on an attitude. Still, several informal reports suggest that prompts like "think
31	carefully" or "you are an expert" slightly improve factual accuracy. If those prompts work through a shared
32	direction, a steering vector along it might improve recall without any task-specific training. This would be
33	useful: a single vector, applied at inference, that makes a model retrieve better.
34	
35	There are reasons to expect this to fail. Function vectors (Todd et al., 2024) show that task information can be
36	carried by a vector, but the vector carries the *task* (antonyms, capitals), not a disposition, and it is extracted
37	from examples of the task itself. Work on the mechanics of factual recall locates the retrieval of an attribute in
38	specific computations at the subject's last token, which a single global direction would have to modulate without
39	knowing the subject. And Liu (2026) finds that fixed linear steering leaves a linearly decodable failure mode in
40	medical QA unchanged across 29 configurations.
41	
42	We find no recall-improving vector. This paper documents the search, in enough detail that the null result is
43	informative: four contrast families, two models, three datasets, three prompt templates, single- and multi-layer
44	injection, two position schemes, and five coefficients spanning the range in which the model stays fluent.
45	
46	## 2 Related work
47	
48	**Steering vectors.** Activation addition (Turner et al., 2023) introduced adding the difference of two prompts'
49	activations at one layer. Contrastive activation addition (Panickssery et al., 2024) averages the difference over
50	many pairs and adds it at all positions after the prompt, steering sycophancy, refusal, hallucination and other
51	behaviours in Llama 2. Representation engineering (Zou et al., 2023) and inference-time intervention (Li et al.,
52	2023) read and steer directions for honesty and truthfulness; the latter improves TruthfulQA, a benchmark that
53	rewards *not* asserting common misconceptions rather than retrieving more facts. Single-direction ablation removes
54	refusal (Arditi et al., 2024).
55	
56	**Prompting for accuracy.** Role prompts ("You are an expert") and instructions to be careful are common in
57	practice. Systematic evaluations of their effect on factual accuracy report small and inconsistent changes. Our
58	§4.4 replicates this for our setting.
59	
60	**Negative results for steering.** Liu (2026) reports a "decodable but not corrected" gap: a failure regime that a
61	probe detects at over 70% balanced accuracy is not corrected by any of five families of fixed linear steering. Our
62	result is of the same kind for a different target: attitudes that are clearly steerable do not carry over to
63	recall.
64	
65	## 3 Method
66	
67	### 3.1 Contrastive pairs
68	
69	For each family we write 64 instruction pairs that differ only in the attitude and share a neutral task. The tasks
70	are unrelated to the evaluation questions: summarising a note, rewriting a sentence, listing ideas, classifying a
71	review. Examples (more in Appendix A):
72	
73	| family | positive | negative |
74	|---|---|---|
75	| careful vs careless | Carefully summarise the following note. | Carelessly summarise the following note. |
76	| confident vs unsure | Confidently list three uses for a paperclip. | Unsurely list three uses for a paperclip. |
77	| expert vs novice | As an expert editor, rewrite this sentence. | As a novice editor, rewrite this sentence. |
78	| focused vs distracted | Stay fully focused and classify this review. | While distracted, classify this review. |
79	
80	The steering vector at layer $l$ is the mean difference of the residual stream at the last instruction token,
81	
82	$$ v_l = \frac{1}{N} \sum_i \left( h_l(x_i^{+}) - h_l(x_i^{-}) \right), $$
83	
84	normalised to unit length. We also tried taking the mean over all instruction tokens instead of the last. It gives
85	vectors with cosine 0.8-0.9 to the last-token ones and the same results, so we report the last-token version.
86	
87	### 3.2 Steering
88	
89	We add $\alpha \, \bar n_l \, \hat v_l$ at a single layer $l$, at every position after the user turn begins, where
90	$\bar n_l$ is the mean residual norm at that layer and $\alpha$ the coefficient. We sweep every fourth layer from 4
91	to 28 and $\alpha \in \{0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2\}$. Coefficients above 0.2 make the outputs visibly degenerate on
92	both models (repetition, language switching), so we stop there.
93	
94	Two variants:
95	- **multi-layer:** the vector added at three adjacent layers at once, with the coefficient divided by three, so the
96	  total added norm matches the single-layer version;
97	- **question-only:** the vector added only at the question's tokens, not at the answer prefix.
98	
99	This gives 7 layers × 5 coefficients × 3 variants = 105 configurations per family and model, 840 in all, each run
100	on 3,000 questions with three templates.
101	
102	### 3.3 Evaluation
103	
104	Closed-book exact match on 1,000 questions each from three QA sets: general trivia, geography, and a medical subset.
105	Each question has a short canonical answer, and we accept a small set of aliases. Decoding is greedy, with a fixed
106	answer format ("Answer with a single word or short phrase."). Each configuration is run with three prompt
107	templates:
108	
109	- **T1:** "Question: {q}\nAnswer:"
110	- **T2:** "{q} Answer with a single word or short phrase."
111	- **T3:** a chat turn with the question as the user message and no system prompt.
112	
113	We report the mean over templates and the spread (minimum and maximum change across templates).
114	
115	### 3.4 Checking that the attitude is steered
116	
117	A null result for recall would be uninteresting if the vectors did nothing at all. We therefore also generate
118	free-form answers to 200 open questions ("Explain how vaccines work.") with and without steering, and ask a judge
119	model which of each pair is more careful, confident, expert or focused (by family), with the order randomised.
120	
121	## 4 Results
122	
123	### 4.1 The best configuration per family
124	
125	**Table 1.** The best single configuration per family and model, chosen on the mean over templates (which favours
126	the vectors).
127	
128	| family | model | best (layer, α, variant) | Δ EM (mean of templates) | spread across templates |
129	|---|---|---|---|---|
130	| careful vs careless | Llama-3.1-8B | (16, 0.05, single) | +0.9 | -0.4 to +2.1 |
131	| confident vs unsure | Llama-3.1-8B | (12, 0.05, multi) | +0.3 | -1.2 to +1.5 |
132	| expert vs novice | Llama-3.1-8B | (16, 0.02, single) | +0.6 | -0.3 to +1.4 |
133	| focused vs distracted | Llama-3.1-8B | (20, 0.05, question) | +0.2 | -0.9 to +1.0 |
134	| careful vs careless | Qwen3.5-9B | (20, 0.05, single) | +0.4 | -0.8 to +1.3 |
135	| confident vs unsure | Qwen3.5-9B | (16, 0.02, multi) | -0.1 | -1.1 to +0.7 |
136	| expert vs novice | Qwen3.5-9B | (20, 0.05, single) | +0.7 | -0.2 to +1.6 |
137	| focused vs distracted | Qwen3.5-9B | (24, 0.05, question) | +0.1 | -1.0 to +1.2 |
138	
139	Run-to-run standard deviation of EM under greedy decoding with shuffled question order is 0.6 points. None of the
140	best configurations clears two standard deviations, and the best layer and coefficient differ by template.
141	Selecting the configuration on one template and testing on the other two gives a mean Δ EM of +0.1.
142	
143	### 4.2 By dataset
144	
145	**Table 2.** Δ EM of the best configuration per family, by dataset (Llama-3.1-8B, mean over templates).
146	
147	| family | trivia | geography | medical |
148	|---|---|---|---|
149	| careful vs careless | +1.1 | +0.6 | +1.0 |
150	| confident vs unsure | +0.4 | -0.2 | +0.7 |
151	| expert vs novice | +0.3 | +0.4 | +1.1 |
152	| focused vs distracted | +0.2 | +0.5 | -0.1 |
153	
154	The medical subset shows slightly larger gains for "expert", which might suggest a domain-specific effect. It does
155	not survive template selection: chosen on T1, the expert vector gives +0.2 on medical with T2 and T3.
156	
157	### 4.3 Coefficient and layer
158	
159	**Table 3.** Δ EM averaged over families, datasets and templates, by layer and coefficient (Llama-3.1-8B,
160	single-layer variant).
161	
162	| layer \ α | 0.01 | 0.02 | 0.05 | 0.1 | 0.2 |
163	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
164	| 4 | 0.0 | +0.1 | -0.2 | -1.4 | -6.8 |
165	| 8 | +0.1 | 0.0 | +0.1 | -1.1 | -5.9 |
166	| 12 | 0.0 | +0.2 | +0.2 | -0.9 | -4.7 |
167	| 16 | +0.1 | +0.2 | +0.3 | -0.6 | -3.9 |
168	| 20 | 0.0 | +0.1 | +0.2 | -0.8 | -4.4 |
169	| 24 | -0.1 | 0.0 | 0.0 | -1.3 | -6.1 |
170	| 28 | 0.0 | -0.1 | -0.3 | -2.2 | -10.9 |
171	
172	Across all families, EM is flat for $\alpha \le 0.05$ and falls for $\alpha \ge 0.1$, by 3-11 points at
173	$\alpha = 0.2$. The fall comes with a rise in malformed answers: at $\alpha = 0.2$, 9-23% of answers are not in the
174	requested format, against under 1% unsteered. There is no regime where recall improves before fluency degrades.
175	Qwen3.5-9B shows the same pattern, with the drop starting slightly earlier (at $\alpha = 0.1$, -1.6 on average).
176	
177	The multi-layer variant spreads the same total push over three layers. It degrades fluency slightly less at
178	$\alpha = 0.2$ (-3.1 on average instead of -5.8) but never improves recall either.
179	
180	### 4.4 Prompting
181	
182	The corresponding prompts ("Answer carefully.", "You are an expert.", "Be confident.", "Focus.") prepended to the
183	question change EM by -0.5 to +1.2 points, also within noise. So the informal reports that motivated this work do
184	not replicate in our setting either, and there was no prompt-level effect for a vector to capture in the first
185	place.
186	
187	### 4.5 Is the attitude actually steered?
188	
189	Yes. The judge rates the steered free-form answers as more careful, confident, expert or focused, in the expected
190	direction, in 71-88% of pairwise comparisons at $\alpha = 0.05$ (Table 4). The effect grows with $\alpha$ until
191	fluency degrades. The vectors change *how* the model answers. They do not change *what* it retrieves.
192	
193	**Table 4.** Judge preference for the steered answer on the family's attribute ($\alpha = 0.05$, best layer).
194	
195	| family | Llama-3.1-8B | Qwen3.5-9B |
196	|---|---|---|
197	| careful vs careless | 0.84 | 0.79 |
198	| confident vs unsure | 0.88 | 0.81 |
199	| expert vs novice | 0.77 | 0.71 |
200	| focused vs distracted | 0.73 | 0.72 |
201	
202	### 4.6 Error analysis
203	
204	We looked at the 50 questions per model whose answer most often changes across configurations. In almost all of
205	them, steering switches between two candidate answers that the unsteered model already ranks first and second, and
206	the switch goes in both directions about equally often. We found no question where steering brings in an answer
207	that the unsteered model does not rank in its top 5. Steering reshuffles near-ties. It does not retrieve.
208	
209	## 5 Discussion
210	
211	Our reading is that retrieval in these models is carried by item-specific features, which a single direction
212	shared across items cannot reach. Behavioural attitudes are a different kind of variable: global, low-dimensional,
213	and easy to push. The judge results show the push lands. The recall results show it lands somewhere that does not
214	feed the retrieval of facts.
215	
216	Two caveats limit how far this generalises. First, we measured recall in the output only. A generic vector could
217	in principle change what the model *represents* at intermediate layers without changing its answer, and we did not
218	look. Second, we stayed within the range of coefficients at which the model remains fluent. We do not rule out
219	that much larger pushes, at layers we did not try, change retrieval in some other way. We do not see a practical
220	use for such a regime, since fluency is already degraded at $\alpha = 0.2$.
221	
222	For practitioners, the result is a warning about the plausible story that "attitude steering makes models better
223	at X". For attitudes and retrieval, it does not, and the small positive numbers that a single sweep produces are
224	noise that does not survive a change of template.
225	
226	## 6 Limitations
227	
228	Two mid-size models and closed-book QA only. Four contrast families, chosen because they correspond to common
229	prompting folklore. We did not try learned or optimised vectors, sparse feature steering, or contrasts outside the
230	four families. We measured recall in the output only, not in the model's intermediate states. Our coefficients are
231	relative to the residual norm at one layer, and our largest total push is 0.2 of that norm.
232	
233	## References
234	
235	- Arditi, A., Obeso, O., Syed, A., Paleka, D., Panickssery, N., Gurnee, W., and Nanda, N. Refusal in language
236	  models is mediated by a single direction. arXiv:2406.11717, 2024.
237	- Li, K., Patel, O., Viégas, F., Pfister, H., and Wattenberg, M. Inference-time intervention: eliciting truthful

# Generic Steering Vectors Do Not Improve Knowledge Recall: A Negative Result

Lucía Herrera, Oren Dahan
Meridian AI Lab

*Preprint, 18 September 2026. Workshop version.*

---

## Abstract

Steering vectors built from contrastive prompt pairs can shift high-level behaviours such as sycophancy or refusal.
A natural hope is that a *generic* steering vector, one that encodes an attitude such as "be careful" or "recall
precisely" rather than any specific fact, could also improve what a model retrieves. We test this hope directly. We
build four families of task-agnostic contrastive vectors (careful vs careless, confident vs unsure, expert vs
novice, and focused vs distracted), sweep the layer, the coefficient and the injection positions, and measure
closed-book recall on three factual QA sets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3.5-9B. The best configuration in
each family changes exact-match accuracy by at most +0.9 points, within run-to-run noise, and no configuration
transfers across prompt templates. Large coefficients degrade fluency before they change recall. The vectors do
change the style of answers as intended, so the null is not a failure to steer. We conclude that generic attitude
vectors do not reach the retrieval process, and we release our sweep so that others need not repeat it.

## 1 Introduction

Contrastive activation addition (Panickssery et al., 2024) and activation addition (Turner et al., 2023) add a
difference-of-means vector to the residual stream to push a model toward one side of a contrast. The resulting
behaviour changes can be large for attributes that the model represents as a direction (Arditi et al., 2024).

Recall is different. Whether a model retrieves the capital of a country, or a drug's mechanism, depends on
specific stored associations, not on an attitude. Still, several informal reports suggest that prompts like "think
carefully" or "you are an expert" slightly improve factual accuracy. If those prompts work through a shared
direction, a steering vector along it might improve recall without any task-specific training. This would be
useful: a single vector, applied at inference, that makes a model retrieve better.

There are reasons to expect this to fail. Function vectors (Todd et al., 2024) show that task information can be
carried by a vector, but the vector carries the *task* (antonyms, capitals), not a disposition, and it is extracted
from examples of the task itself. Work on the mechanics of factual recall locates the retrieval of an attribute in
specific computations at the subject's last token, which a single global direction would have to modulate without
knowing the subject. And Liu (2026) finds that fixed linear steering leaves a linearly decodable failure mode in
medical QA unchanged across 29 configurations.

We find no recall-improving vector. This paper documents the search, in enough detail that the null result is
informative: four contrast families, two models, three datasets, three prompt templates, single- and multi-layer
injection, two position schemes, and five coefficients spanning the range in which the model stays fluent.

## 2 Related work

**Steering vectors.** Activation addition (Turner et al., 2023) introduced adding the difference of two prompts'
activations at one layer. Contrastive activation addition (Panickssery et al., 2024) averages the difference over
many pairs and adds it at all positions after the prompt, steering sycophancy, refusal, hallucination and other
behaviours in Llama 2. Representation engineering (Zou et al., 2023) and inference-time intervention (Li et al.,
2023) read and steer directions for honesty and truthfulness; the latter improves TruthfulQA, a benchmark that
rewards *not* asserting common misconceptions rather than retrieving more facts. Single-direction ablation removes
refusal (Arditi et al., 2024).

**Prompting for accuracy.** Role prompts ("You are an expert") and instructions to be careful are common in
practice. Systematic evaluations of their effect on factual accuracy report small and inconsistent changes. Our
§4.4 replicates this for our setting.

**Negative results for steering.** Liu (2026) reports a "decodable but not corrected" gap: a failure regime that a
probe detects at over 70% balanced accuracy is not corrected by any of five families of fixed linear steering. Our
result is of the same kind for a different target: attitudes that are clearly steerable do not carry over to
recall.

## 3 Method

### 3.1 Contrastive pairs

For each family we write 64 instruction pairs that differ only in the attitude and share a neutral task. The tasks
are unrelated to the evaluation questions: summarising a note, rewriting a sentence, listing ideas, classifying a
review. Examples (more in Appendix A):

| family | positive | negative |
|---|---|---|
| careful vs careless | Carefully summarise the following note. | Carelessly summarise the following note. |
| confident vs unsure | Confidently list three uses for a paperclip. | Unsurely list three uses for a paperclip. |
| expert vs novice | As an expert editor, rewrite this sentence. | As a novice editor, rewrite this sentence. |
| focused vs distracted | Stay fully focused and classify this review. | While distracted, classify this review. |

The steering vector at layer $l$ is the mean difference of the residual stream at the last instruction token,

$$ v_l = \frac{1}{N} \sum_i \left( h_l(x_i^{+}) - h_l(x_i^{-}) \right), $$

normalised to unit length. We also tried taking the mean over all instruction tokens instead of the last. It gives
vectors with cosine 0.8-0.9 to the last-token ones and the same results, so we report the last-token version.

### 3.2 Steering

We add $\alpha \, \bar n_l \, \hat v_l$ at a single layer $l$, at every position after the user turn begins, where
$\bar n_l$ is the mean residual norm at that layer and $\alpha$ the coefficient. We sweep every fourth layer from 4
to 28 and $\alpha \in \{0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2\}$. Coefficients above 0.2 make the outputs visibly degenerate on
both models (repetition, language switching), so we stop there.

Two variants:
- **multi-layer:** the vector added at three adjacent layers at once, with the coefficient divided by three, so the
  total added norm matches the single-layer version;
- **question-only:** the vector added only at the question's tokens, not at the answer prefix.

This gives 7 layers × 5 coefficients × 3 variants = 105 configurations per family and model, 840 in all, each run
on 3,000 questions with three templates.

### 3.3 Evaluation

Closed-book exact match on 1,000 questions each from three QA sets: general trivia, geography, and a medical subset.
Each question has a short canonical answer, and we accept a small set of aliases. Decoding is greedy, with a fixed
answer format ("Answer with a single word or short phrase."). Each configuration is run with three prompt
templates:

- **T1:** "Question: {q}\nAnswer:"
- **T2:** "{q} Answer with a single word or short phrase."
- **T3:** a chat turn with the question as the user message and no system prompt.

We report the mean over templates and the spread (minimum and maximum change across templates).

### 3.4 Checking that the attitude is steered

A null result for recall would be uninteresting if the vectors did nothing at all. We therefore also generate
free-form answers to 200 open questions ("Explain how vaccines work.") with and without steering, and ask a judge
model which of each pair is more careful, confident, expert or focused (by family), with the order randomised.

## 4 Results

### 4.1 The best configuration per family

**Table 1.** The best single configuration per family and model, chosen on the mean over templates (which favours
the vectors).

| family | model | best (layer, α, variant) | Δ EM (mean of templates) | spread across templates |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| careful vs careless | Llama-3.1-8B | (16, 0.05, single) | +0.9 | -0.4 to +2.1 |
| confident vs unsure | Llama-3.1-8B | (12, 0.05, multi) | +0.3 | -1.2 to +1.5 |
| expert vs novice | Llama-3.1-8B | (16, 0.02, single) | +0.6 | -0.3 to +1.4 |
| focused vs distracted | Llama-3.1-8B | (20, 0.05, question) | +0.2 | -0.9 to +1.0 |
| careful vs careless | Qwen3.5-9B | (20, 0.05, single) | +0.4 | -0.8 to +1.3 |
| confident vs unsure | Qwen3.5-9B | (16, 0.02, multi) | -0.1 | -1.1 to +0.7 |
| expert vs novice | Qwen3.5-9B | (20, 0.05, single) | +0.7 | -0.2 to +1.6 |
| focused vs distracted | Qwen3.5-9B | (24, 0.05, question) | +0.1 | -1.0 to +1.2 |

Run-to-run standard deviation of EM under greedy decoding with shuffled question order is 0.6 points. None of the
best configurations clears two standard deviations, and the best layer and coefficient differ by template.
Selecting the configuration on one template and testing on the other two gives a mean Δ EM of +0.1.

### 4.2 By dataset

**Table 2.** Δ EM of the best configuration per family, by dataset (Llama-3.1-8B, mean over templates).

| family | trivia | geography | medical |
|---|---|---|---|
| careful vs careless | +1.1 | +0.6 | +1.0 |
| confident vs unsure | +0.4 | -0.2 | +0.7 |
| expert vs novice | +0.3 | +0.4 | +1.1 |
| focused vs distracted | +0.2 | +0.5 | -0.1 |

The medical subset shows slightly larger gains for "expert", which might suggest a domain-specific effect. It does
not survive template selection: chosen on T1, the expert vector gives +0.2 on medical with T2 and T3.

### 4.3 Coefficient and layer

**Table 3.** Δ EM averaged over families, datasets and templates, by layer and coefficient (Llama-3.1-8B,
single-layer variant).

| layer \ α | 0.01 | 0.02 | 0.05 | 0.1 | 0.2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 0.0 | +0.1 | -0.2 | -1.4 | -6.8 |
| 8 | +0.1 | 0.0 | +0.1 | -1.1 | -5.9 |
| 12 | 0.0 | +0.2 | +0.2 | -0.9 | -4.7 |
| 16 | +0.1 | +0.2 | +0.3 | -0.6 | -3.9 |
| 20 | 0.0 | +0.1 | +0.2 | -0.8 | -4.4 |
| 24 | -0.1 | 0.0 | 0.0 | -1.3 | -6.1 |
| 28 | 0.0 | -0.1 | -0.3 | -2.2 | -10.9 |

Across all families, EM is flat for $\alpha \le 0.05$ and falls for $\alpha \ge 0.1$, by 3-11 points at
$\alpha = 0.2$. The fall comes with a rise in malformed answers: at $\alpha = 0.2$, 9-23% of answers are not in the
requested format, against under 1% unsteered. There is no regime where recall improves before fluency degrades.
Qwen3.5-9B shows the same pattern, with the drop starting slightly earlier (at $\alpha = 0.1$, -1.6 on average).

The multi-layer variant spreads the same total push over three layers. It degrades fluency slightly less at
$\alpha = 0.2$ (-3.1 on average instead of -5.8) but never improves recall either.

### 4.4 Prompting

The corresponding prompts ("Answer carefully.", "You are an expert.", "Be confident.", "Focus.") prepended to the
question change EM by -0.5 to +1.2 points, also within noise. So the informal reports that motivated this work do
not replicate in our setting either, and there was no prompt-level effect for a vector to capture in the first
place.

### 4.5 Is the attitude actually steered?

Yes. The judge rates the steered free-form answers as more careful, confident, expert or focused, in the expected
direction, in 71-88% of pairwise comparisons at $\alpha = 0.05$ (Table 4). The effect grows with $\alpha$ until
fluency degrades. The vectors change *how* the model answers. They do not change *what* it retrieves.

**Table 4.** Judge preference for the steered answer on the family's attribute ($\alpha = 0.05$, best layer).

| family | Llama-3.1-8B | Qwen3.5-9B |
|---|---|---|
| careful vs careless | 0.84 | 0.79 |
| confident vs unsure | 0.88 | 0.81 |
| expert vs novice | 0.77 | 0.71 |
| focused vs distracted | 0.73 | 0.72 |

### 4.6 Error analysis

We looked at the 50 questions per model whose answer most often changes across configurations. In almost all of
them, steering switches between two candidate answers that the unsteered model already ranks first and second, and
the switch goes in both directions about equally often. We found no question where steering brings in an answer
that the unsteered model does not rank in its top 5. Steering reshuffles near-ties. It does not retrieve.

## 5 Discussion

Our reading is that retrieval in these models is carried by item-specific features, which a single direction
shared across items cannot reach. Behavioural attitudes are a different kind of variable: global, low-dimensional,
and easy to push. The judge results show the push lands. The recall results show it lands somewhere that does not
feed the retrieval of facts.

Two caveats limit how far this generalises. First, we measured recall in the output only. A generic vector could
in principle change what the model *represents* at intermediate layers without changing its answer, and we did not
look. Second, we stayed within the range of coefficients at which the model remains fluent. We do not rule out
that much larger pushes, at layers we did not try, change retrieval in some other way. We do not see a practical
use for such a regime, since fluency is already degraded at $\alpha = 0.2$.

For practitioners, the result is a warning about the plausible story that "attitude steering makes models better
at X". For attitudes and retrieval, it does not, and the small positive numbers that a single sweep produces are
noise that does not survive a change of template.

## 6 Limitations

Two mid-size models and closed-book QA only. Four contrast families, chosen because they correspond to common
prompting folklore. We did not try learned or optimised vectors, sparse feature steering, or contrasts outside the
four families. We measured recall in the output only, not in the model's intermediate states. Our coefficients are
relative to the residual norm at one layer, and our largest total push is 0.2 of that norm.

## References

- Arditi, A., Obeso, O., Syed, A., Paleka, D., Panickssery, N., Gurnee, W., and Nanda, N. Refusal in language
  models is mediated by a single direction. arXiv:2406.11717, 2024.
- Li, K., Patel, O., Viégas, F., Pfister, H., and Wattenberg, M. Inference-time intervention: eliciting truthful
  answers from a language model. arXiv:2306.03341, 2023.
- Liu, M. Decodable but not corrected by fixed residual-stream linear steering: evidence from medical LLM failure
  regimes. arXiv:2605.05715, 2026.
- Panickssery, N., Gabrieli, N., Schulz, J., Tong, M., Hubinger, E., and Turner, A. M. Steering Llama 2 via
  contrastive activation addition. arXiv:2312.06681, 2024.
- Todd, E., Li, M. L., Sen Sharma, A., Mueller, A., Wallace, B. C., and Bau, D. Function vectors in large language
  models. arXiv:2310.15213, 2024.
- Turner, A. M., Thiergart, L., Leech, G., Udell, D., Vazquez, J. J., Mini, U., and MacDiarmid, M. Steering
  language models with activation engineering. arXiv:2308.10248, 2023.
- Zou, A., Phan, L., Chen, S., Campbell, J., Guo, P., Ren, R., Pan, A., Yin, X., Mazeika, M., Dombrowski, A.-K.,
  et al. Representation engineering: a top-down approach to AI transparency. arXiv:2310.01405, 2023.

"""The single-token basic families: the bank judge with the any-layer item rule."""

from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

from wsbench.banks import exact_targets, item_targets, load_bank
from wsbench.basic.judge import CellKey, JudgeOutcome, judge_cells
from wsbench.basic.prompts import PROMPT_VERSION
from wsbench.cache import Cache
from wsbench.family import pass_rate_result, require_cells, tri_state
from wsbench.judge_config import JudgeConfig
from wsbench.llm import Spend
from wsbench.mcjudge import Preflighter, item_scope, with_readout_count
from wsbench.readouts import Cell, load_readouts
from wsbench.registry import REPO_ROOT, EvalSpec, JudgeArgs
from wsbench.results import FamilyResult

GROUP = "basic"
CHANCE_LABEL = "no analytic floor (free text); the prompt-only baseline is the measured floor"


def bank_family(name: str, title: str, *, n_items: int = 100, n_layers: int = 11) -> EvalSpec:
    bank = Path("evals") / name / "items.json"
    return EvalSpec(
        name=name,
        title=title,
        group=GROUP,
        bank=bank,
        judge=JudgeConfig(prompt_version=PROMPT_VERSION),
        metric="pass_rate",
        higher_is_better=True,
        run=lambda args: run_family(args, name=name, bank=REPO_ROOT / bank),
        calls_per_arm=f"≈ {n_items * n_layers / 1000:.1f}k",
        sources="",
    )


def targets_of(item: dict[str, Any]) -> list[str]:
    return exact_targets(item_targets(item))


def group_cells(cells: list[Cell]) -> dict[CellKey, list[Cell]]:
    groups: dict[CellKey, list[Cell]] = defaultdict(list)
    for c in cells:
        groups[(c.id, c.layer)].append(c)
    return dict(groups)


def run_family(args: JudgeArgs, *, name: str, bank: Path) -> FamilyResult:
    _header, items = load_bank(bank)
    scope = item_scope(items, args)
    ids = [it["id"] for it in scope]
    targets = {it["id"]: targets_of(it) for it in scope}
    cells, rep = load_readouts(args.readouts, ids=ids, layers=args.layers)
    layers = args.layers if args.layers is not None else rep.layers
    groups = group_cells(cells)
    expected = [(i, layer) for i in ids for layer in layers]
    missing = [k for k in expected if k not in groups]
    require_cells(name, missing, len(expected), args)

    spend = Spend()
    with Cache(args.out / "cells.jsonl") as cache:
        outcome = judge_cells(
            groups,
            targets,
            kind=rep.kind or "prose",
            judge=args.judge,
            cache=cache,
            spend=spend,
            preflight=Preflighter(args.dry_run),
            concurrency=args.concurrency,
            rpm=args.rpm,
            dry_run=args.dry_run,
        )

    rows = [_item_row(i, layers, groups, targets[i], outcome) for i in ids]
    result = pass_rate_result(
        name=name,
        args=args,
        prompt_version=PROMPT_VERSION,
        rows=rows,
        cells=cells,
        rep=rep,
        # a cell is one (item, layer) judge call; empty = every sample at that layer is blank
        n_expected=len(expected),
        n_missing=len(missing),
        n_unjudged=outcome.n_unjudged,
        n_empty=outcome.n_empty,
        spend=spend,
        chance_label=CHANCE_LABEL,
        config_extra={"layers_judged": layers},
        extras={"n_calls": outcome.n_calls},
    )
    return with_readout_count(result, scope, cells)


def _item_row(
    item_id: str,
    layers: list[int],
    groups: dict[CellKey, list[Cell]],
    targets: list[str],
    outcome: JudgeOutcome,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """``pass`` is True on any expressed layer, False when every expected layer was judged
    negative, and None (undecided) when nothing is expressed and a layer is missing or
    unjudged."""
    per_layer: dict[str, dict[str, Any]] = {}
    expressed_layers: list[int] = []
    n_unjudged = n_missing = 0
    for layer in layers:
        cells = groups.get((item_id, layer))
        if cells is None:
            n_missing += 1
            continue
        verdict = outcome.verdicts.get((item_id, layer))
        if verdict is None:
            n_unjudged += 1
        elif verdict.expressed:
            expressed_layers.append(layer)
        per_layer[str(layer)] = verdict.to_json() if verdict is not None else {"expressed": None}
    undecided = n_unjudged > 0 or n_missing > 0 or not per_layer
    return {
        "id": item_id,
        "targets": targets,
        "pass": tri_state(bool(expressed_layers), undecided),
        "earliest_layer": min(expressed_layers) if expressed_layers else None,
        "n_unjudged": n_unjudged,
        "n_missing": n_missing,
        "layers": per_layer,
    }

    result = pass_rate_result(
        name=name,
        args=args,
        prompt_version=PROMPT_VERSION,
        rows=rows,
        cells=cells,
        rep=rep,
        # a cell is one (item, layer) judge call; empty = every sample at that layer is blank
        n_expected=len(expected),
        n_missing=len(missing),
        n_unjudged=outcome.n_unjudged,
        n_empty=outcome.n_empty,
        spend=spend,
        chance_label=CHANCE_LABEL,
        config_extra={"layers_judged": layers},
        extras={"n_calls": outcome.n_calls},
    )
    return with_readout_count(result, scope, cells)


def _item_row(
    item_id: str,
    layers: list[int],
    groups: dict[CellKey, list[Cell]],
    targets: list[str],
    outcome: JudgeOutcome,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """``pass`` is True on any expressed layer, False when every expected layer was judged
    negative, and None (undecided) when nothing is expressed and a layer is missing or
    unjudged."""
    per_layer: dict[str, dict[str, Any]] = {}
    expressed_layers: list[int] = []
    n_unjudged = n_missing = 0
    for layer in layers:
        cells = groups.get((item_id, layer))
        if cells is None:
            n_missing += 1
            continue
        verdict = outcome.verdicts.get((item_id, layer))
        if verdict is None:
            n_unjudged += 1
        elif verdict.expressed:
            expressed_layers.append(layer)
        per_layer[str(layer)] = verdict.to_json() if verdict is not None else {"expressed": None}
    undecided = n_unjudged > 0 or n_missing > 0 or not per_layer
    return {
        "id": item_id,
        "targets": targets,
        "pass": tri_state(bool(expressed_layers), undecided),
        "earliest_layer": min(expressed_layers) if expressed_layers else None,
        "n_unjudged": n_unjudged,
        "n_missing": n_missing,
        "layers": per_layer,
    }

87	def resolve(rule: dict[str, Any], tokens: list[str]) -> list[int]:
88	    """Token indices a rule selects over ``tokens`` (the render's token strings, byte-level BPE
89	    display or plain). Every kind above is handled; unknown kinds raise."""
90	    n = len(tokens)
91	    kind = rule["kind"]
92	    if kind == "final_token":
93	        return [n - 1] if n else []
94	    if kind == "offset_from_end":
95	        k = int(rule["k"])
96	        return [-k] if 0 < k <= n else []
97	    if kind == "last_n":
98	        return list(range(max(0, n - int(rule["n"])), n))
99	    if kind == "all":
100	        return list(range(n))
101	    if kind == "all_from_end":
102	        return list(range(-n, 0))
103	    if kind == "positions":
104	        return [int(p) for p in rule["positions"] if 0 <= int(p) < n]
105	    if kind == "line_one_newline":

107	        return [nls[-1]] if nls else []
108	    if kind == "from_token":

110	        hits = [i for i, t in enumerate(tokens) if _clean(t) == want or t == want]
111	        return list(range(hits[0], n)) if hits else []
112	    if kind == "from_last_sentence_start":

114	    if kind in ("suffix_text", "suffix_text_then_tail"):

125	def _from_last_sentence_start(tokens: list[str]) -> list[int]:

129	        i

131	        if t == "<|im_start|>" and i + 1 < n and tokens[i + 1] == "user"
132	    ]
133	    if not starts or not ends:

136	    u1 = next((e for e in ends if e > u0), n)
137	    body = list(range(u0 + 3, u1))  # skip <|im_start|>, user, newline
138	    if not body:

443	        return [

449	                GRID,

452	            )

459	    return sorted(
460	        p.name
461	        for p in (REPO_ROOT / "evals").iterdir()
462	        if (p / "items.json").exists() or (p / "manifest.json").exists()
463	    )

466	def write(specs: Iterable[ReadSpec], path: Path) -> int:
467	    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
468	    n = 0
469	    with path.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
470	        for s in specs:
471	            fh.write(json.dumps(s.row(), ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
472	            n += 1
473	    return n
